The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Apply [F2] using [A3], collecting all matter-independent quadratic gauge terms, including any initially written in $F_\lambda$, into $P_{\mathrm{kin},\lambda}$. The numerical constant of the remainder is fixed by [A3], since $P_{\mathrm{kin}}(0)=0$. Thus every hypothesis needed for the supplier's nonkinetic F-term conclusion holds, and $F_{\mathrm{rem},\lambda}=F_{\mathrm{rem},\Lambda_0}$ coefficientwise. Every collected quadratic term vanishes at $W=0$, so $F_\lambda(\Phi,0)=F_{\mathrm{rem},\lambda}(\Phi,0)$ at each scale. Evaluating the remainder identity at $W=0$ and restricting to the fixed light-field variables gives $W_\lambda(\Phi)=W_{\Lambda_0}(\Phi)$.

The map $P_{\mathrm{hol}}$ is the same linear coordinate projection at both scales by [A2]. Applying it to the equality in step 1.1 gives $P_{\mathrm{hol}}W_\lambda=P_{\mathrm{hol}}W_{\Lambda_0}$. Since the retained operators are a fixed ordered basis, equality of their coordinate vectors gives equality of each retained coefficient.

The gauge-coupling correction and the freedom of the real D-term are exactly the exceptions in [F2]. The conclusion concerns the fixed Wilsonian holomorphic coordinates, so it does not imply equality of one-particle-irreducible vertices or of coefficients after a scale-dependent field rescaling; the formal perturbative hypothesis in [A3] also excludes nonperturbative and continuum conclusions.

Use the mostly-plus metric and the matrices $\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}$ specified by the four-dimensional super-Poincare algebra. A **chiral superfield** is an even element $\Phi\in\mathscr S$ satisfying the two equations

$$\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\Phi=0,\qquad \bar D_{\dot\alpha}:=-\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}-i\sum_{\alpha,\mu}\theta^\alpha\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}\partial_\mu,\quad \dot\alpha\in\{\dot1,\dot2\}.$$

For a smooth coefficient function $f$, $f(y)$ means the finite Taylor substitution $\sum_{k=0}^{2}(\Delta y^{\mu_1}\cdots\Delta y^{\mu_k}/k!)\,\partial_{\mu_1}\cdots\partial_{\mu_k}f(x)$, with the $k=0$ term equal to $f(x)$ and repeated spacetime indices summed; higher terms vanish in $\Lambda_4$. $$\Phi(y,\theta)=A(y)+\theta^1\psi_1(y)+\theta^2\psi_2(y)+\theta^1\theta^2F(y).$$

Set $\mathscr S_\epsilon=C^\infty(\mathbb R^{1,3},\mathcal A_\epsilon\widehat\otimes\Lambda_4)$ and embed $\mathscr S$ into it by $a\mapsto a\otimes1$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
